name: Stoicism
era: c. 300 BCE to 180 CE, revived today
line: Live by reason. Accept what is not up to you.

quote.text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.

quotes.text: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.
Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.
It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it.
If it is not right, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it.

words.usage: The only thing the Stoics call good without qualification.
Epictetus: the one thing that cannot be taken from you.
Judgment, impulse, desire and aversion. The opening line of the Enchiridion.

words.meaning: The reason that orders the world
words.usage: Also the reason in you. To live well is to bring the two into agreement.
What appears to you before you have judged it.
Saying yes to an impression. The moment where freedom lives.

words.meaning: The ruling faculty; the commanding part of the mind
words.usage: Marcus addresses his own constantly.
Not apathy. The sage still feels; they are not dragged.

words.meaning: A passion: an excessive impulse born of a false judgment
words.usage: Four families: distress, fear, craving, and irrational delight.
Joy, caution and wishing: the feelings that follow true judgments.
Health, wealth, reputation, even life. Neither good nor bad in themselves.
Things worth choosing, such as health, without needing them to be happy.

words.meaning: An appropriate action; what befits your role
words.usage: Cicero rendered it as officium, duty.

words.meaning: Appropriation; widening what you treat as your own
words.usage: From self, to family, to city, to all people.

words.meaning: The mutual interdependence of all things
words.usage: Marcus: what harms the hive harms the bee.
For Stoics, virtue is sufficient for it.
First of the four cardinal virtues: knowing what is truly good, bad and neither.
Giving each person what is due, including kindness.
Knowing what is and is not worth fearing.
Order in what you choose and what you leave.
Musonius Rufus: philosophy is learned by habit, like medicine or music.

words.meaning: Attention to oneself in the present moment
words.usage: The basic Stoic attitude, in Pierre Hadot’s reading.
Plan fully, then add: fate permitting.
A Cynic word the Stoics made their own.
An ideal, as rare as the phoenix. Everyone else is "making progress".
What a practicing Stoic actually is.
The school is named after the Painted Porch where Zeno taught in public.
Seneca: what is foreseen arrives more gently.
Seneca’s Latin for the Greek euthymia.

words.meaning: Leisure given to study and reflection
words.usage: For Seneca, leisure without study is death.
A later Latin phrase for an old Stoic exercise, the practice of death.
Coined by Nietzsche in 1882, not by a Stoic, though it echoes Epictetus and Marcus.

practices.name: Morning premeditation
practices.instructions: Before you look at a screen, sit up and name the day ahead. Who will you meet? What could go wrong: a delay, a criticism, a temptation? Picture each one plainly, then picture yourself meeting it with patience and good sense. End with the reserve clause: I will do this today, if nothing prevents me.
practices.why: Marcus Aurelius opens Book 2 this way: today I will meet the meddling and the ungrateful. Seneca adds that the blow you foresee lands softer. The point is readiness, not pessimism.
variations: Write three lines instead of thinking them.
Rehearse one specific conversation you are dreading.
On a calm day, rehearse losing something you rely on.

practices.name: Cold shower
practices.instructions: End your shower with cold water. Start with thirty seconds and breathe slowly through the first shock. Notice the judgment "this is unbearable" and watch it turn out to be false. Skip this if you have a heart condition or feel unwell.
practices.why: Seneca called himself a cold-water enthusiast and plunged into the Virgo aqueduct on the first of January. Chosen discomfort teaches the body that it can obey you.
variations: Wash your face and forearms in cold water.
A brisk walk without a coat on a cool day.
Full cold for two minutes once thirty seconds is easy.

practices.name: Voluntary discomfort
practices.instructions: Pick one comfort and go without it until evening: skip a meal or eat it plain, leave the coffee, take the stairs, sit on the floor. While you go without, ask Seneca’s question: is this what I was afraid of?
practices.why: Seneca, Letter 18: set aside days when you are content with the scantiest and cheapest fare. You practice poverty so that fortune cannot frighten you with it.
variations: Plain bread and water for lunch.
No phone from noon to six.
Wear your oldest clothes for the day.

practices.name: Evening review
practices.instructions: When the house is quiet, go back through the day from waking. Ask three questions. What did I do badly? What did I do well? What did I leave undone? Be a fair judge, not a prosecutor: note it, decide what to do tomorrow, and let it go.
practices.why: Seneca describes doing this every night once the light was out, a habit he learned from Sextius. Epictetus quotes the same three questions from the Pythagorean Golden Verses.
variations: Write it in your commonplace book.
Review only your reactions to other people.
End by naming one thing you will do differently tomorrow.

practices.name: Dichotomy check
practices.instructions: Write down what is worrying you right now, one item per line. Next to each, mark it "mine" if it is a judgment, intention or action of yours, and "not mine" if it depends on other people, the body, money or luck. For each "mine", write one thing you will do. For each "not mine", write: "this is not up to me, and I will meet it calmly."
practices.why: The Enchiridion opens with this split. Most distress comes from spending effort on the second column and neglecting the first.
variations: Do it out loud while walking.
Only sort the three biggest worries.
Add a third column for what you can influence but not control.

tasks.name: Read a page of Meditations, then answer it
tasks.meta: Read · Marcus wrote it for himself

tasks.name: Take In Our Time: Stoicism for a walk
Evening audit: what was up to you today?
Put your biggest annoyance through the dichotomy of control
Eat like a Stoic: bread, olives and cheese, no screen
Take the stairs and enjoy it on purpose
Watch the sunrise or the first light with nothing in your hands
Wear your plainest clothes today and notice who cares
Tell a friend which line of Marcus you would put on a wall
Pick one person you will be patient with today
Do one task fully, without commentary
tasks.meta: The task in front of you

rules.text: Complain to no one, not even yourself
rules.why: Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 8.9) says let no one hear you blaming palace life, not even yourself. Grumbling is rehearsal: you get good at whatever you practise, and complaint rehearses the judgment that something bad has happened.

rules.text: Catch the first jolt and name the judgment
rules.why: Epictetus tells you to say to every harsh impression: you are an impression and not at all what you appear to be. The pause between the jolt and your reply is where assent can be withheld.

rules.text: Choose one small discomfort a day
rules.why: Skip the second coffee, take the stairs, finish the shower cold. This is training, not punishment: chosen hardships make the unchosen ones smaller.

rules.text: Eat with your phone in another room
rules.why: A meal is the easiest place to give something your whole mind, and the Stoics treated attention as the thing you actually own.

rules.text: Say what is needed, in few words
rules.why: Epictetus (Enchiridion 33): let silence be the general rule, or say only what is necessary, and briefly. Narrating your whole day is optional. Skipping it is a workout.

rules.text: Do the next right thing in your role
rules.why: Parent, colleague, neighbour, citizen. The Stoics measured a day by duties met, not by feelings had. Ask what the role in front of you asks, then do that.

read.title: Meditations
read.creator: Marcus Aurelius, trans. Gregory Hays
read.why: Private notes to himself, written in Greek on campaign. Read a few entries at a time.

read.title: Letters from a Stoic
read.creator: Seneca, trans. Robin Campbell
read.why: Letters to his friend Lucilius: warm, practical and full of exercises.

read.title: Enchiridion
read.creator: Epictetus, recorded by Arrian
read.why: The handbook. Short enough to read in an hour and reread for a lifetime.

read.title: Discourses
read.creator: Epictetus, recorded by Arrian
read.why: The classroom itself: blunt, funny and unsparing.

read.title: On the Shortness of Life
read.creator: Seneca
read.why: Life is long enough if you know how to use it.

read.title: Lectures and Sayings
read.creator: Musonius Rufus, trans. Cynthia King
read.why: Epictetus’s teacher on food, work, marriage and why women should study philosophy.

read.title: The Inner Citadel
read.creator: Pierre Hadot
read.why: The best study of the Meditations as a set of spiritual exercises.

read.title: Courage Under Fire
read.creator: James B. Stockdale
read.why: A navy pilot on how Epictetus carried him through seven years as a prisoner of war.

read.title: How to Think Like a Roman Emperor
read.creator: Donald Robertson
read.why: A therapist reads Marcus alongside modern cognitive therapy.

watch.title: Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations: The Stoic Ideal
watch.creator: Michael Sugrue (lecture)
watch.why: Forty-five minutes that have sent a great many people to the book.

watch.title: The Fall of the Roman Empire
watch.creator: Anthony Mann
watch.why: Alec Guinness as Marcus on the Danube frontier. Epic, and looser with history than it looks.

watch.title: Gladiator
watch.creator: Ridley Scott
watch.why: Richard Harris as the old emperor. Fiction, but the opening winter camp sets the mood.

listen.title: In Our Time: Stoicism
listen.creator: BBC Radio 4, Melvyn Bragg
listen.why: Three scholars on the school from Zeno to Marcus.

listen.title: In Our Time: Marcus Aurelius
listen.creator: BBC Radio 4, Melvyn Bragg
listen.why: The man, the reign and the notebook.

listen.title: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps: the Stoics
listen.creator: Peter Adamson
listen.why: A run of short episodes on Stoic logic, physics and ethics.

listen.title: Seikilos epitaph
listen.creator: Anonymous, Tralles
listen.why: The oldest complete song that survives. Its words: while you live, shine; life is short.

listen.title: Meditations, read aloud
listen.creator: Any unabridged recording
listen.why: One book a day, on a walk.

art.title: Equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius
art.creator: Capitoline Museums, Rome
art.why: The only bronze equestrian statue of an emperor to survive. His hand is open, not armed.

art.title: Column of Marcus Aurelius
art.creator: Piazza Colonna, Rome
art.why: A spiral relief of the Danube wars he wrote the Meditations during.

art.title: The Death of Seneca
art.creator: Peter Paul Rubens
art.why: Seneca in the bath, dictating to the end. Alte Pinakothek, Munich.

art.title: Stoa of Attalos
art.creator: Ancient Agora, Athens
art.why: A reconstructed stoa a short walk from where the Painted Porch stood.

art.title: Roman portrait busts
art.creator: Any museum collection
art.why: Look for the tired, unflattered faces of the late Republic.

eat.title: Bread, olives and cheese
eat.creator: Greek and Roman staple
eat.why: Simple, eaten slowly, with nothing else going on.

eat.title: Lentil soup
eat.creator: A plain pot
eat.why: The Cynic Crates made the young Zeno carry a pot of lentil soup through Athens to cure his shame.

eat.title: Green figs
eat.creator: Fresh or dried
eat.why: Diogenes Laertius says Zeno was fond of green figs.

eat.title: Barley porridge
eat.creator: Puls, the food of early Rome
eat.why: What Roman soldiers and farmers lived on before bread.

eat.title: One plain meal
eat.creator: Musonius Rufus, Lecture 18
eat.why: Food that is cheap, easy to get and needs no cook.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: For a full day
drink.why: Epictetus: drink water, and do not tell everyone that you drink water.

drink.title: Wine mixed with water
drink.creator: Greek and Roman custom
drink.why: Wine was drunk diluted. Unmixed wine was thought barbarous.

drink.title: Posca
drink.creator: Roman soldiers’ drink
drink.why: Water sharpened with wine vinegar. Cheap, sour and reviving.

customs.title: Plan for obstacles at dawn
customs.creator: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.1
customs.why: Begin the day expecting difficult people, and decide in advance not to be made worse by them.

customs.title: Keep a commonplace book
customs.creator: Hypomnēmata
customs.why: Copy lines worth keeping by hand. The Meditations began as one.

customs.title: Review the day at night
customs.creator: Seneca, On Anger 3.36
customs.why: Examine your whole day before sleep, hiding nothing from yourself.

customs.title: Practice poverty for a few days
customs.creator: Seneca, Letter 18
customs.why: Coarse food, rough clothes, and the question: is this what I feared?

customs.title: Take the view from above
customs.creator: Meditations 9.30
customs.why: Look down on cities, armies, weddings and funerals as if from a height.

customs.title: Walk and talk
customs.creator: The Stoa Poikile
customs.why: The school met in a public walkway, not behind walls. Think on your feet.

games.title: Ludus latrunculorum
games.creator: Board game · Roman
games.why: The Roman game of little soldiers: pieces are captured by flanking them on two sides. Seneca mentions men absorbed in it. Rules are reconstructed, so agree yours before you start.

games.title: Knucklebones
games.creator: Dexterity game · Greek and Roman
games.why: Five small bones or stones, tossed and caught on the back of the hand. A game of chance that Stoics used as a picture of life: you do not choose the throw, only how you play it.

games.title: Assassin’s Creed Odyssey: Discovery Tour
games.creator: Video game · Ubisoft Quebec
games.why: A combat-free walk through classical Greece with guided tours, including the Athenian agora where the painted porch stood. Earlier than Zeno by a century, and still the best way to see the setting.

games.title: Old World
games.creator: Video game · Mohawk Games
games.why: A strategy game of ancient dynasties in which rulers age, fail and die. Good practice in the Stoic view of fortune: plan well, then accept the event.

festivals.title: Stoic Week
festivals.creator: Each autumn, online
festivals.why: A free seven-day course run since 2012 by the Modern Stoicism group. Thousands of people follow the same daily exercises and compare notes.

festivals.title: Saturnalia
festivals.creator: 17 December and the days after
festivals.why: The Roman midwinter festival of feasting and role reversal. Seneca used it in Letter 18 as the moment to practise eating plainly while the city overdid it.

festivals.title: Stoicon
festivals.creator: Once a year, usually in autumn
festivals.why: The annual conference on Stoicism as a way of life, held in a different city or online, with talks by scholars and practitioners.

places.title: The Painted Porch
places.creator: Ancient Agora, Athens, Greece
places.why: The foundations of the Stoa Poikile, where Zeno taught and which gave the school its name, lie at the north edge of the Agora beside Adrianou Street.

places.title: Stoa of Attalos
places.creator: Ancient Agora, Athens, Greece
places.why: A full reconstruction of a Hellenistic stoa, now the Agora museum. Walk its colonnade to feel what teaching in a porch was like.

places.title: Equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius
places.creator: Capitoline Museums, Rome, Italy
places.why: The only large bronze of a Roman emperor on horseback to survive. The original is indoors; a copy stands on the Capitoline square.

places.title: Carnuntum
places.creator: Lower Austria
places.why: The Danube frontier camp where Marcus Aurelius spent years on campaign. The heading of Book 3 of the Meditations reads: written at Carnuntum.

places.title: Nicopolis
places.creator: Near Preveza, Epirus, Greece
places.why: The city where Epictetus set up his school after philosophers were expelled from Rome. Its walls, theatre and museum can be visited.

ethics.title: Virtue is the only good
ethics.text: Wisdom, justice, courage and temperance. Everything else, including health and money, is preferred or not, but never good or bad in itself.
ethics.practice: When you want something today, ask which virtue it serves.

ethics.title: We are made for each other
ethics.text: Marcus: we were born to work together, like feet, hands and eyelids. To turn against another person is against nature.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today for someone who cannot repay it, and tell no one.

ethics.title: Accept what you cannot change
ethics.text: Meet what happens with a steady mind and do your part. Acceptance is the start of action, not the end of it.
ethics.practice: Name one fact you have been arguing with. Stop arguing; ask what it asks of you.

ethics.title: Play your role well
ethics.text: You did not choose the part: child, parent, citizen, neighbor. Playing it well is up to you.
ethics.practice: List your roles. Pick the one you have neglected and do its next duty.

ethics.title: Widen the circle
ethics.text: Hierocles drew concentric circles from the self outward to all humanity, and asked us to draw each one in.
ethics.practice: Treat a stranger today with the courtesy you keep for friends.

ethics.title: Anger is a brief madness
ethics.text: Seneca held that anger is never useful, even in a just cause. Reason does the work better and stops when the work is done.
ethics.practice: When anger rises, delay. Seneca’s first remedy is time.

philosophy.title: The dichotomy of control
philosophy.text: Some things are up to you: judgment, intention, desire, aversion. The rest is not: your body, property, reputation, office. Confuse the two and you will be hindered and upset.
philosophy.practice: Before any worry, sort it: mine to decide, or not?

philosophy.title: The view from above
philosophy.text: Imagine your life from far overhead: the street, the city, the turning earth. Most troubles shrink to their real size.
philosophy.practice: Write one page describing today as seen from orbit.

philosophy.title: Memento mori
philosophy.text: Death is not far off and not an evil. Holding it in view strips the day of triviality.
philosophy.practice: When you say goodnight to someone, remember quietly that it is not guaranteed again.

philosophy.title: Premeditation of evils
philosophy.text: Rehearse what could go wrong so it cannot surprise you. Familiar things lose their sting.
philosophy.practice: Take the thing you most fear this week and walk through it step by step.

philosophy.title: Impressions and assent
philosophy.text: Things appear to you already wearing a judgment. You may decline to agree. This gap is the whole of Stoic freedom.
philosophy.practice: Catch one "this is terrible" today and restate it as bare fact.

philosophy.title: Living according to nature
philosophy.text: To live well is to live in agreement with reason, your own and the world’s. For a human being that means thinking clearly and acting for the common good.
philosophy.practice: Ask of one decision: what would a reasonable, sociable creature do here?

philosophy.title: The obstacle becomes the way
philosophy.text: The mind adapts and converts to its own purposes whatever blocks it. A setback is material for patience, courage or inventiveness.
philosophy.practice: Pick today’s main obstacle and name the virtue it lets you practice.

philosophy.title: The present is all you have
philosophy.text: No one loses any life but the one they are living now. The past and the future are not yours to hold.
philosophy.practice: Give ten minutes to one task as if nothing else existed.

philosophy.title: The inner citadel
philosophy.text: Nothing outside can enter the ruling part of the mind unless it opens the gate. You can retreat there at any moment.
philosophy.practice: Three times today, stop and take one slow breath inside the citadel.

philosophy.title: The discipline of desire
philosophy.text: Want only what depends on you and you will never be disappointed. Want anything else and you hand your peace to chance.
philosophy.practice: Notice one craving. Wait twenty minutes. See what remains.

dayThemes: We are made for each other
A good death, a good day

intro: Stoicism is a practical philosophy of life. It teaches that we suffer less from events than from the judgments we add to them, and that a good character is enough for a good life.

It began around 300 BCE, when Zeno, a merchant from Cyprus who had lost his cargo in a shipwreck, started teaching in a public colonnade on the edge of the Athenian marketplace. The colonnade was the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, and his students were called Stoics after it. For five centuries it was among the most influential schools of the Greek and Roman world, taught to slaves and senators alike.

The early Stoics divided philosophy into three parts. Logic trained the mind to tell true impressions from false ones. Physics described a single living cosmos, ordered throughout by reason, the logos, of which each human mind is a fragment. Ethics drew the conclusion: since reason is our nature, the good life is a life in agreement with it. They compared the three to an orchard, with logic the wall, physics the trees and ethics the fruit.

Their central claim is severe and freeing at once. Only virtue is good: wisdom, justice, courage and temperance. Only vice is bad. Everything else, including health, wealth, reputation and life itself, is "indifferent". Some indifferents are naturally worth choosing, but none can make you happy or miserable. What can is how you use them, and that is always up to you.

Almost nothing survives from the founders. What we read today comes from three Romans of the first and second centuries: Seneca, a statesman who wrote letters on how to live; Epictetus, a former slave whose classes were written down by a student; and Marcus Aurelius, an emperor who kept a notebook for himself. They care less about theory than about practice. Their pages are full of exercises: rehearse the day at dawn, examine it at night, picture what you could lose, go without on purpose, pause before you agree to an impression.

Stoicism faded as a school in the third century but never left. Christian writers borrowed its language, Renaissance scholars revived it, and the founders of cognitive behavioural therapy named Epictetus as a source. This Onda follows the Roman approach: you will not study Stoicism so much as train in it, a day at a time.
guide.era: c. 300 BCE to 180 CE, revived today

figures.name: Zeno of Citium
figures.bio: Founder. A Phoenician merchant from Cyprus who studied under the Cynic Crates and taught at the Painted Porch that gave the school its name.

figures.name: Cleanthes
figures.bio: Zeno’s successor. A former boxer who carried water at night to pay for his studies. His Hymn to Zeus survives.

figures.name: Chrysippus
figures.bio: Third head of the school and its great systematizer, credited with more than 700 works. The ancients said: no Chrysippus, no Stoa.

figures.name: Panaetius of Rhodes
figures.bio: Brought Stoicism to the Roman elite and softened it for people with public duties. Cicero’s On Duties leans on him.

figures.name: Cato the Younger
figures.bio: Roman senator who lived the philosophy more than he wrote it. His death at Utica made him the model Stoic for centuries.

figures.name: Seneca
figures.bio: Statesman, playwright and tutor to Nero. Wrote essays and 124 letters on how to live. Ordered to kill himself in 65.

figures.name: Musonius Rufus
figures.bio: Called the Roman Socrates. Exiled more than once. Taught that philosophy is practice and that women should study it too.

figures.name: Epictetus
figures.bio: Born into slavery in Phrygia, freed in Rome, later ran a school at Nicopolis. Taught that freedom lives in your own choices.

figures.name: Marcus Aurelius
figures.bio: Roman emperor from 161. His private notes, written in Greek during the Danube wars, became the Meditations.

figures.name: Hierocles
figures.bio: Known for the image of concentric circles: draw each wider circle of people toward the centre.

history.what: Zeno begins teaching at the Stoa Poikile in Athens
history.detail: After a shipwreck cost him his cargo, Zeno read about Socrates in a bookshop, studied for years under several teachers, and then taught in the open air. The school took its name from the porch, stoa in Greek.
He held the school together for three decades and gave Stoic theology its most famous text, the Hymn to Zeus.

history.what: Chrysippus becomes head and systematizes the school
history.detail: He developed propositional logic and defended Stoic ethics against the sceptical Academy. Most later Stoic doctrine is his.

history.what: An embassy of philosophers brings Stoicism to Rome
history.detail: Athens sent three philosophers, among them the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon, to argue a fine before the Senate. Their public lectures caused a sensation.

history.what: Panaetius joins the circle of Scipio Aemilianus
history.detail: Middle Stoicism takes shape: less about the perfect sage, more about ordinary people making progress.

history.what: Cato the Younger dies at Utica
history.detail: Rather than accept pardon from Julius Caesar, Cato took his own life after reading Plato’s Phaedo. Later Stoics treated him as proof the philosophy could be lived.
Not a Stoic himself, Cicero preserved a great deal of Stoic ethics in Latin and coined much of its vocabulary.
Banished by Claudius, he wrote consolations to his mother and others. Recalled in 49, he became tutor and then adviser to the young Nero.

history.what: Seneca writes the Letters to Lucilius
history.detail: Withdrawn from court, he wrote 124 letters in three years. In 65, accused of joining a plot, he was ordered to die and opened his veins.

history.what: Domitian banishes the philosophers from Rome
history.detail: Epictetus left for Nicopolis in north-western Greece and opened a school there that drew students from across the empire.

history.what: Arrian records the Discourses of Epictetus
history.detail: Epictetus wrote nothing. His student Arrian took down the classes and later distilled them into the Enchiridion, the handbook.
Two books are headed "among the Quadi" and "at Carnuntum", camps on the Danube frontier. He died on campaign in 180.
No head of the Stoa is recorded after this. Its ideas pass into Neoplatonism and early Christian ethics.
The Flemish scholar launched Neostoicism, an attempt to join Stoic ethics with Christian belief during the wars of religion.
Albert Ellis and later Aaron Beck built therapies on the idea that beliefs, not events, cause distress, and both cited Epictetus.
Academics and therapists at the University of Exeter invited the public to live as a Stoic for seven days and measured the result. It has run every year since.

concepts.text: Moral excellence, the one thing fully in your control.
concepts.detail: The four cardinal virtues are wisdom, justice, courage and temperance. The Stoics held that they are really one thing, knowledge of how to live, seen from four sides. You cannot have one without the others.

concepts.text: Health, wealth and reputation. Preferred, but never the point.
concepts.detail: Calling them indifferent does not mean not caring. It means they cannot make a life good or bad. A wise person chooses health over sickness when it is on offer and loses nothing essential when it is not.

concepts.text: Impressions arrive uninvited. What you agree to is your choice.
concepts.detail: An impression says "I have been insulted". Assent adds "and that is a bad thing that has happened to me". Emotion follows the assent, not the impression. Training attention on that moment is the core of Stoic practice.

concepts.text: Excessive impulses that come from false judgments about good and bad.
concepts.detail: There are four families: distress and delight about the present, fear and craving about the future. The cure is not suppression but correcting the judgment underneath.

concepts.text: The emotions that follow true judgments.
concepts.detail: The sage is not numb. In place of delight there is joy; in place of fear, caution; in place of craving, a reasonable wishing. There is no good counterpart to distress.

concepts.text: All things are connected in one living whole.
concepts.detail: The Stoic cosmos is a single organism pervaded by reason. Nothing happens in isolation, which is why harming another person is a kind of self-harm.

concepts.text: The natural widening of what you care for as your own.
concepts.detail: A newborn cares for itself, then its parents, then its city. Reason asks you to keep going until the circle holds every human being.

concepts.text: Everything is caused; your character is one of the causes.
concepts.detail: Chrysippus compared us to a cylinder pushed down a slope. The push comes from outside, but it rolls as it does because of its own shape. What happens is fated; how you meet it is yours.

Epictetus organised training into three fields: wanting only what depends on you, acting well toward others, and judging impressions carefully. Pierre Hadot showed the Meditations follows the same plan.

concepts.text: The Stoic formula for the goal of life.
concepts.detail: Not a call to the countryside. Human nature is rational and social, so to follow nature is to think truthfully and act for the common good.

facts.text: The word stoic comes from the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, a public colonnade decorated with battle scenes. Its foundations were found in the Athenian Agora in 1981.
Marcus Aurelius never meant the Meditations to be read. The title is not his; the manuscript tradition calls it "To Himself".
Epictetus was lame. One ancient source says his master broke his leg; another says he was lame from childhood.
Zeno said of his shipwreck: I made a prosperous voyage when I was wrecked.
Cleanthes paid for philosophy by drawing water for gardens at night. Athenians nicknamed him the Well-Drawer.
Chrysippus is said to have died laughing at his own joke, after seeing a donkey eat his figs.
Seneca was among the richest men in Rome, and his critics never let him forget it. He replied that a wise man does not love wealth but prefers to have it.
Admiral James Stockdale, shot down over Vietnam in 1965, credited Epictetus for surviving more than seven years as a prisoner of war.
Stoic logic, long overlooked in favour of Aristotle’s, anticipated the propositional logic developed in the nineteenth century.

glossary.meaning: The Painted Porch in Athens where the school began.
The perfectly wise person. An ideal to steer by rather than a claim anyone made.
Arrian’s record of Epictetus teaching. Four of eight books survive.
Greek for handbook: Arrian’s short digest of Epictetus.
The sixteenth-century revival led by Justus Lipsius.
The school of Diogenes that taught Zeno: virtue is enough, convention is nothing.
